hardware.title: PCB Design & Board Bring-up
hardware.description: From schematic to a board that boots, with hardware and firmware under one roof.
hardware.longDescription: We design boards in KiCad (power paths, battery charging, USB-C, ESP32 and RP2040) and bring them up: first power-on, clocks, peripherals and drivers. Because the same team does the hardware and the firmware, nobody has to guess which side a bug is on.
points: KiCad schematic and layout, 2 and 4 layers
Production files for JLCPCB: Gerbers, BOM and pick-and-place
Bring-up, first drivers and a written bring-up report

firmware.title: RTOS & Embedded Linux Firmware
firmware.description: Firmware and connectivity that stay up in the field.
firmware.longDescription: FreeRTOS on Cortex-M and ESP32, embedded Linux on Raspberry Pi and custom hardware, and the connectivity in between: Ethernet, Wi-Fi and MQTT. We write the drivers, chase down the hard bugs (memory, timing, networking) and leave you with code your team can maintain.
points: Drivers, RTOS tasks and protocol stacks
Ethernet, Wi-Fi and MQTT device-to-cloud links
Debugging crashes, memory leaks and timing issues
firmware.proof: Core developers of a production i.MX RT IoT gateway, with 199 releases shipped since 2025.

updates.title: Secure Updates & CRA Readiness
updates.description: Field updates that can’t brick a device, ready for the Cyber Resilience Act.
updates.longDescription: Since September 2026 the EU Cyber Resilience Act requires manufacturers to report actively exploited vulnerabilities, and from December 2027 connected products must ship with secure updates, an SBOM and a defined support period. We build the update path (signed images, A/B slots, automatic rollback) and set up the SBOM and vulnerability-handling process around it.
points: CRA gap assessment with a prioritized roadmap
Signed A/B updates with automatic rollback
SBOM generated in CI and a vulnerability-handling runbook
updates.proof: Built over-the-air bootloader and firmware updates for a production IoT gateway, and an A/B loader with automatic rollback for a Raspberry Pi kiosk fleet.

modernization.title: Firmware Modernization
modernization.description: Make legacy firmware testable, maintainable and safe to change.
modernization.longDescription: Old toolchains, no tests, and one person who understands the code. We audit legacy firmware, move it step by step to modern C++ (or Rust where it fits), and add tests that run on a PC and on real hardware in CI, so changes stop being scary.
points: Code audit with a prioritized report
Host-side unit tests and hardware-in-the-loop tests in CI
Incremental rewrites to modern C++ or Rust
modernization.proof: Built hardware-in-the-loop update tests that run in Jenkins on every change to a production IoT gateway.

ai.title: AI for Engineering Teams
ai.description: Get your firmware team productive with AI coding tools, with every change still verified on real hardware.
ai.longDescription: Hands-on workshops and repository setup for embedded teams adopting tools like Claude Code and GitHub Copilot: project knowledge files, review guardrails, and workflows where every AI-made change is verified on real hardware. Also available: Software Engineering in Practice, a three-part training on foundations, resilience and production.
points: Workshop on AI-assisted embedded development
Repository setup: agent instructions, knowledge bases and guardrails
Software Engineering in Practice training with certificates
ai.proof: Set up the agent instructions and knowledge base for a production firmware project, now used day to day by its developers.

fintech.title: FinTech & Payment Systems
fintech.description: Payment terminals, vending machines and kiosks that handle money reliably.
fintech.longDescription: Payment and vending devices have to work every time: a failed transaction costs money and trust. We build firmware for payment terminals, vending machines and self-service kiosks, covering payment flows, stock tracking, secure communication and field updates that don’t take a machine offline.

manufacturing.title: Industrial & Manufacturing
manufacturing.description: Connected machines that report what they’re doing and keep running.
manufacturing.longDescription: Factory equipment runs for years and can’t stop for a firmware bug. We build controllers and gateways that collect machine data, send it over Ethernet or MQTT, and keep running through power cuts, network drops and updates.

defense.title: Defense & Aerospace
defense.description: Predictable, verifiable software for high-stakes programs.
defense.longDescription: In defense and aerospace, software has to be predictable, tested and documented. We bring experience from avionics programs (deterministic real-time behaviour, rigorous testing and traceable documentation) to every project.

automotive.title: Automotive & Mobility
automotive.description: Firmware and lab tooling for vehicle development.
automotive.longDescription: Vehicle development runs on tooling that has to work every time: flashing, netbooting and test benches. Our open-source TFTP server and client are used by automotive engineers, and we build firmware and lab tooling with real-time and reliability requirements in mind.

kiosk.title: Field updates that can’t brick a device
kiosk.challenge: A fleet of Raspberry Pi kiosks needed remote updates and provisioning, with nobody on site to recover a device when an update goes wrong.
kiosk.work: Built the loader that supervises the kiosk software: A/B app slots with automatic rollback after repeated failures, a 21-step provisioning script that is safe to re-run, a systemd watchdog, and a Jenkins + Docker pipeline that checks every release before it ships.
kiosk.result: 18 releases over 18 months, each rolled out remotely and rolled back automatically if it fails.

tftpd.title: A TFTP server automotive engineers build on
tftpd.challenge: U-Boot netbooting and board flashing need a small, dependable TFTP server and client that runs on any machine in the lab.
tftpd.work: Wrote rs-tftpd from scratch in pure Rust, with RFC 2347–2349 and 7440 option support and a matching client, and maintain it as an open-source project.
tftpd.result: Packaged for NixOS and openSUSE, with contributions from engineers at Renault Software Labs, Ampere and Nokia. Renault uses the client as a library, and its duplicate-packets option cut an Apache NuttX network boot from 4 minutes to 20 seconds.

hardware.servicesTitle: Four ways we take risk out of your board.

review.label: Design review in 48 hours
review.lead: A second pair of eyes on your schematic and layout, with the datasheets open.
review.text: Send us your KiCad project, or the schematic and Gerbers. Within 48 hours you get a written review of the schematic, the layout and an EMC pre-compliance pass. Every finding names the part, the pin or the board location, cites the datasheet line it rests on and says how to fix it. The price is fixed and agreed before we start.
points: Schematic checked against the datasheets: pin functions, ratings, strap pins, supply sequencing
Layout checked for power paths, return paths, decoupling, fab rules and assembly
EMC pre-compliance screening with located findings
A written report with coordinates and a fix for each finding
review.proof: On the Paper Calendar the EMC pass found 6 warnings on a board that already had no errors, each with its coordinates and a fix.
callouts: A via where an SPI line changes layer, 7 mm from the nearest return-path capacitor
42 mm of board edge without a ground via
The e-paper booster loop, about 2.6 nH

board.label: Idea to orderable board
board.lead: From a requirements description to files you can send to the fab.
board.text: Describe what the board has to do. We turn it into a verified design: a schematic with checked parts, a routed layout and fabrication files designed to order with the fab’s standard options, so nothing special has to be explained to the fab. Prototypes can come assembled.
points: ERC and DRC clean, with schematic and board proven to match
Design-for-manufacture checks against JLCPCB’s capabilities
EMC screening before release
Gerbers, BOM and placement files, with parts picked from what is in stock
An assembled prototype delivered to you
board.proof: The Paper Calendar: a 4-layer ESP32-S3 board with a 50-pin e-paper connector, charger, fuel gauge and audio amplifier, in manufacturing at JLCPCB since October 2026.

firmware.label: Firmware tested before the board exists
firmware.lead: Your real firmware, running against your circuit, weeks before boards arrive.
firmware.text: Our emulator runs the firmware image you will flash on a model of the microcontroller, wired to a model of your board built from its circuit: pull-ups, buttons, regulators, fuel gauge, display controller. Scripted scenarios press buttons, drain the battery, cut the network or let days pass, and assert what the pins, buses, console and display did. Each CPU core is checked instruction by instruction against QEMU.
points: ESP32-S3 and ESP32-C3, RP2040, i.MX RT1024 with Ethernet, AVR
Scenarios for power, buttons, network and display
Pixel-exact checks of what the display shows
Runs headless, so it becomes a check in your CI
firmware.proof: The Paper Calendar’s production firmware boots end to end in the emulator: 7 scenarios and 68 assertions pass, including the exact image on the e-paper.
firmware.caption: What the real firmware drew on the emulated e-paper at first boot, and its console output.
firmware.screenLabel: The 800 × 480 image the circuit’s panel model received, pixel for pixel

emc.label: EMC, SI and PI pre-compliance
emc.lead: Find what the compliance lab would find, while a fix is still cheap.
emc.text: Our own field solvers, written for circuit boards, look at what rules of thumb miss: 2D cross-sections for impedance and crosstalk, the impedance of a power plane pair with your real decoupling capacitors, return current around slots and plane gaps, and a GPU 3D full-wave solver for the critical regions. Findings come with exact locations and fixes. These are pre-compliance estimates that reduce the risk of a lab visit. They are not certification.
points: Trace impedance and crosstalk from the real stackup
Power-network impedance against a target, with the capacitors you placed
Return current and the loop inductance a slot adds
3D full-wave fields for the regions that matter
emc.proof: Measured against references: single traces within 0.3 % of the textbook formulas, stripline within 0.001 % of the exact solution, plane resonances within 0.06 % of the analytic cavity. On differential pairs with real copper it showed that the common closed-form formula reads 4 to 13 % low, confirmed with openEMS.
emc.slotCaption: A trace crossing a 20 mm slot in the ground plane (synthetic example). The current detours around the slot: it adds 2.3 nH and 0.15 V of noise for a 3.3 V, 1 ns edge.
emc.pdnCaption: The 3V3 rail seen from the ESP32-S3 with the board’s real decoupling: above the 0.66 ohm target from 136 MHz, peaking at 2.3 ohm.
emc.fdtdCaption: The electric field 0.8 mm above the board at 1 GHz, where the EPD_SCK line changes layer, from our own 3D full-wave solver (the inner planes simplified as solid).

hardware.mapText: The EMC screen of the Paper Calendar on its real copper: six numbered warnings and 23 information items, each at its coordinates. Nothing is a guess about “the board”: every finding points at a place you can open in your layout tool.
hardware.caseLead: Our own e-paper calendar: ESP32-S3, 4 layers, in manufacturing at JLCPCB.
hardware.caseText: We built it with the toolchain we use for customers, so we know what it finds and what it misses. The design came out of our checks with no errors. Its firmware runs end to end in the emulator against its own circuit. Its EMC screen then found what a normal review would not look for.

caseFacts.label: scenarios / assertions passing in the emulator
EMC warnings, each with coordinates and a fix

findings: Five vias where the e-paper SPI lines change layer are 6.2 to 9.5 mm from the nearest stitching capacitor (limit 3 mm at a 1 ns edge). Fix: a 100 nF capacitor within 3 mm of each, or one routing layer.
42 mm of the top edge has no ground via. Fix: two or three ground vias.
The 3V3 plane impedance first exceeds its 0.66 ohm target at 136 MHz at the ESP32-S3, where the module’s own decoupling takes over.
checked: No fast net crosses a gap in its reference plane
Every supply pin has its capacitor within 5 mm
The e-paper booster loops are about 2.6 nH and return in the plane
hardware.caseNote: The warnings assume a 1 ns edge, the screen’s floor. Measuring the real edge on the first boards settles them, and that is how we hand findings over: what is known, what is assumed and how to settle it.
